summary.text: A standard candle is an astronomical object that has a known luminosity.
By comparing that known luminosity with an object's observed brightness, astronomers compute its distance using the inverse-square law.
Several methods on the cosmic distance ladder rely on them, and each rung of the ladder gives information used to find the next.

items.prompt: Two street lamps are known to use the same bulb, but one looks much fainter. What does that tell you?

options.label: The fainter lamp is farther away
The fainter lamp is a weaker bulb
The fainter lamp is on a taller pole
The fainter lamp is switched on for fewer hours

items.explain: Comparing known luminosity with observed brightness gives distance by the inverse-square law.

items.prompt: Astronomers find a new class of exploding star and want to use it as a yardstick. What must they pin down first?

options.label: Its colour, measured from a single bright member
Its age, taken from the oldest member they see
Its true brightness, found from members at well-known distances
Its speed, estimated from members in the same cluster

items.explain: Calibration means determining the candle's exact absolute magnitude, which needs enough members of the class with well-known distances.

items.prompt: Why is it risky to use a standard candle's brightness on a very distant object?

options.label: The candle's brightness changes whenever it is observed
It may not truly belong to the class, giving a wrong distance
Distant objects are always brighter than nearby ones
The inverse-square law stops working beyond a set range

items.explain: Recognising members of the class is a problem, and at extreme distances it can be quite serious.

items.prompt: In the 1950s astronomers learned that the nearby stars used for calibration were a different type from those in nearby galaxies. What happened to distance estimates?

options.label: They roughly halved for nearby galaxies and the Milky Way
They stayed the same but became more precise
They could no longer be made for nearby galaxies
They roughly doubled for nearby galaxies and the Milky Way's size

items.explain: The distant population II stars were much brighter than believed, which doubled estimates of distance to globular clusters, nearby galaxies and the Milky Way's diameter.

items.prompt: Why do astronomers use a ladder of methods rather than one technique?

options.label: No single technique can measure distances at every range
Each method gives the same answer, so they check one another
Each method works only on one kind of star
One method would take longer than a human lifetime

items.explain: Because no single technique works at all ranges, each rung gives information used to determine the next higher rung.

items.prompt: By watching a gravitational wave's waveform, astronomers can work out the power of its source. What does that make the source?

options.label: A standard siren of known loudness
A source whose colour reveals its age
A source of unknown brightness that can never be used for distance
A fixed rung at the base of the ladder with no assumptions

items.explain: Observing the waveform gives the chirp mass and thence the power, so such a source is a standard siren of known loudness.
